1801.content: Verify webhook authenticity using HMAC-SHA256 signatures

1825.content: All webhook requests from Seal include an HMAC-SHA256 signature in the Seal-Signature header. Always verify this signature to ensure the request is authentic and hasn't been tampered with.

1826.content: Without signature verification, anyone who knows your webhook URL could send fake events to your endpoint. Signature verification ensures:

1827.content: Authenticity: The request came from Seal

1828.content: Integrity: The payload hasn't been modified

1831.content:
Security Critical: Never process webhook events without verifying the signature. Unverified
webhooks are a security vulnerability.

1832.content: Seal generates an HMAC-SHA256 hash of the request body using your webhook secret

1833.content: The hash is sent in the Seal-Signature header

1834.content: Your server generates the same hash using the same secret

1835.content: If the hashes match, the request is authentic

1836.content: The signature is computed on the raw request body, not the parsed JSON. Make sure to:

1837.content: Access the raw body before parsing

1840.content: Always use timing-safe comparison functions to prevent timing attacks:

1844.content: Always check if the signature header exists:

1845.content: When rotating secrets, support both old and new secrets temporarily:

1846.content: Always Verify: Never skip signature verification, even in development

1847.content: Use HTTPS: Webhook URLs must use HTTPS in production

1848.content: Rotate Secrets: Rotate webhook secrets every 90 days

1849.content: Store Securely: Keep secrets in environment variables or secrets manager

1850.content: Log Failures: Monitor and alert on signature verification failures

1851.content: Rate Limit: Implement rate limiting on webhook endpoints

1852.content: Validate Payload: Verify payload structure after signature check

1853.content: Check Secret: Ensure you're using the correct webhook secret (not API key)

1854.content: Check Encoding: Verify you're using UTF-8 encoding

The Seal API is organized around REST principles. Our API has predictable resource-oriented URLs, accepts JSON-encoded request bodies, returns JSON-encoded responses, and uses standard HTTP response codes, authentication, and verbs.
The Seal API is organized into the following resource categories:
The Seal API uses Clerk API keys for authentication. All API requests must include a valid API key in the Authorization header.
The Seal API uses query-parameter-based routing for resource operations. Since the underlying Convex HTTP router does not support path parameters, resource IDs are passed as query parameters:
The Seal API uses REST over HTTPS with JSON request and response bodies. Authentication is handled via Clerk API keys passed in the Authorization header.
The Seal API uses standard HTTP status codes and returns detailed error responses following RFC 7807 (Problem Details for HTTP APIs) to help you diagnose and handle errors effectively.

The Seal MCP (Model Context Protocol) server enables AI assistants like Claude to interact with your Seal account directly. This allows for AI-powered document workflows, automated signing processes, and intelligent document management.
The Seal MCP server provides 27 tools that give AI assistants complete access to your Seal account. All tools require OAuth authentication and respect your organization's permissions.
The Seal MCP server uses Clerk OAuth 2.0 for secure authentication. This guide walks you through configuring OAuth access for AI assistants.
